# My Honda Accord Shuts Off While Driving: A Fuel System Diagnosis

When a vehicle suddenly cuts out while in motion, it is an urgent safety issue that demands immediate attention. In your specific caseâa 2005 Honda Accordâthe symptoms of accelerating for several hours followed by an abrupt shutdown, combined with the fact that the engine restarts after sitting for a few minutes, point strongly toward a fuel delivery problem rather than an electrical failure. If the car were suffering from a complete loss of power generation (like a blown alternator or a seized starter), it would likely not restart immediately upon turning the key. The ability to crank and run suggests the ignition system and battery are functional; the issue lies in the supply chain feeding those systems.

The most probable culprit is contaminated fuel. Introducing gas from an unfamiliar source into a high-mileage engine introduces significant risk. Older vehicles, particularly those manufactured around 2005, often lack modern filtration standards found in newer models. Fuel pumps designed to last 150,000 miles on premium ethanol-free gasoline can be devastated by ethanol blends containing water or sediment within minutes of exposure. Ethanol is hygroscopic, meaning it attracts moisture from the air, which separates out and settles at the bottom of the tank as a distinct layer of water. When your car accelerates, this heavy sludge hits the fuel pump pickup first. Once the impeller spins against this mixture, cavitation occurs, and the pump loses prime, cutting power to the injectors instantly.

To verify this hypothesis without expensive diagnostic tools, perform a visual inspection of the fuel filter. On the 2005 Accord, the in-line fuel filter is typically located under the vehicle on the driver's side, near the fuel tank filler neck. Locate the clamp securing the hose and inspect the mesh element. If it appears dark black or clogged with debris, you have confirmed contamination. However, visual inspection alone does not rule out water separation in the pump itself.

The immediate steps to stop this malfunction are procedural and mechanical. First, do not attempt to drive the car again until the tank is drained. Attempting to run on fumes or low fuel levels after a contamination event can draw sediment from the bottom of the tank directly into the intake manifold. Safely tow the vehicle to a reputable mechanic. Request that they perform a fuel system flush and replace the inline fuel filter. This is not an optional maintenance item in this scenario; it is a critical repair to prevent catastrophic failure of the fuel pump motor.

If the fuel filter replacement does not resolve the issue, the next step involves checking the fuel pressure regulator and the fuel pump relay. The 2005 Accord uses a specific relay strategy where the engine control module (ECM) controls the pump prime circuit. If the ECM detects low voltage or erratic resistance from the fuel rail due to water in the lines, it may cut power to prevent engine damage, causing the stall. You can check this by listening for the distinct "click-click" sound of the fuel pump priming when you turn the key to the "ON" position before cranking. If there is no sound, trace the circuit back to the relay in the under-hood fuse box.

Replacing the fuel filter and draining the contaminated fuel are the necessary steps to restore reliability. Ignoring this issue risks burning out the expensive high-pressure fuel pump or damaging the catalytic converter with unburned fuel caused by lean conditions from a starving injectors. The lesson here is clear: when the source of your fuel changes, verify the quality before committing to a long drive.

For developers looking at system stability, this scenario mirrors handling bad input data. You cannot debug a crash if you don't stop feeding the system corrupted inputs first. The fix requires isolating and replacing the compromised component (the filter) before continuing operation with clean inputs.
